title: Standard Normal Distributions
p: Before beginning, please enter your name here, otherwise I won't know who you are based on the default assigned name. Alternatively, you can opt to create an account but this isn't necessary.

The standard normal distribution is the name that is given to the familiar bell-shaped curve in statistics. It is an example of a continuous distribution, meaning that it is defined based on a function, and you can calculate a probability at any point within the domain of that function.
It is generally not necessary for you to know this, but the function that draws the shape of a standard normal distribution is: f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2}
If you have a graphing calculator nearby, or can access Desmos, try graphing this function to convince yourself that it does in fact draw a bell curve.

definition: Standard Normal Distribution The standard normal distribution is a normal distribution that has a mean of zero, and a standard deviation of one.

section.title: Locating the Mean of a Normal Distribution
section.p: You can easily determine the location of the mean of a normal distribution by its graph because the highest point locates the mean. Take a look at the graph of the standard normal distibution above, and notice that the peak is located at zero, meaning that the mean of that distribution is zero.

section.title: Estimating the Standard Deviation of a Normal Distribution
section.p: It is not as easy to determine the value of the standard deviation of a normal distribution by simply looking at the graph, but it can usually be estimated by judging where the peak of the curve stops looking like a downward facing parabola, and begins to look like an upward facing curve. In calculus, we learn the name of this point is called an inflection point, and on the normal distribution, there are two of these points. They are located a little higher than halfway between the peak of the curve and the horizontal axis.
The graph below highlights these points so you can get a visual idea of where these are located.

section.p: These points are located one unit away from the mean, so one is the value of the standard deviation. Try moving the slider below to see the effect on the shape of the graph for different values of the standrad deviation.

section:
Calculating probabilities
For any continuous probability distribution, we define the associated probability as the area under the curve from as far left as possible, up to a given value. This is known as the cumulative area under the curve, and is by default situated on the left-end of the distribution. Mathematical formulas exist to calculate this area, but the computations are often very involved and thus we rely on technology to do this for us.
On a standard normal distribution, it is common to name the horizontal axis the z-axis, as opposed to the x-axis, as this ties in the relationship between z-scores and normal distributions, which we will explore in a later section. This region that defines the probability is always illustrated as a shaded region between the curve and the z-axis. We use the following notation to indicate the area of this region: P(Z < a) = \text{cumulative area under the curve up to } z=a
Drag the point along the axis below to see how the shaded region changes based on different values of z. The area of the shaded region, which defines the probability, is also shown below.
A graph that allows the user to experience visually what is meant by an area to the left of a given z-score on a standard normal distribution for different values of z.
1/sqrt(2pi)*e^(-0.5*x^2)
y = 0
(0,0) $axisline
P(Z < round($Z0.x,2)) = round($$normalcdf($Z0.x),4)
The total area under a continuous distribution function is equal to one, and because the normal distribution is perfectly symmetric, there is 50% of the area to the left of the mean, and 50% to the right.

Depending on what you are using to calculate your normal distribution probabilities, you may or may not have the ability to calculate a right-tail (the area to the right of a given z-score) directly. This is not a problem, however, because in continuous distributions like the normal distribution, left-tail and right-tail probabilities are complementary. This means that: P(Z > a) = 1 - P(Z < a) As long as you can calculate a left-tail probability, you will also be able to calculate a right-tail probability. Click on the toggle buttons to see visually how these regions are complementary.
Another property you can see here is that the probabilitiy of a single outcome in a continuous distribution is always zero, because there is no region at a single point to calculate an area. You can click on this item in the chart above to see this as well. Using our notation for probabilities, this looks like: P(Z = a) = 0

section:
Area Between Example The area between two z-scores is notated as: P(a < Z < b) and is interpreted as: P(Z > a) \text{ and } P(z < b) If we choose two particular z-scores, such as z=-0.82 and z=1.12, then we visualize this region as:
A pictoral representation of the area under the curve of the normal distribution graph between z=-0.82 to z = 1.12. The user can toggle on and off different regions in order to understand the relationships among the areas.
$$normalpdf(x, 0, 1)
Show P(Z < -0.82)
Show P(Z < 1.12)
Show P(-0.82 < Z < 1.12)
As with right-tailed probabilities, you may or may not be able to calculate the area between two z-scores directly, but you can calculate the area between two scores by finding the left-tail area associated with the larger z-score and subtracting the area of the smaller z-score. This means that assuming b > a: P(a < Z < b) = P(z < b) - P(z < a) Use the graph above that demonstrates the areas associated between, and to the left of two different z-scores to convince yourself that this is true, and then verify it by answering the following questions. Use three decimal places of accuracy.
Area to the left of the larger z-score: P(Z < 1.12)=
round($btwex1,3) = 0.869 abs($btwex1 - 0.869) <= $probtol abs($btwex1 - (1-.869)) <= $probtol
Area to the left of the smaller z score: P(Z < -0.82)=
round($btwex2,3) = 0.206 abs($btwex2 - 0.206) <= $probtol abs($btwex2 - (1-0.206)) <= $probtol
Now subtract these two values to get the area between them: P(-0.82 < Z < 1.12) =
round($btwex3,3) = 0.663 round($btwex3,3) = -0.663
Be careful and ensure you are rounding your answer correctly. You are on the right track, but you may have calculated a right-tail probability instead of a left-tail.
